title: Chapter XXIV

teacherSummary.text: Walton resumes writing. The ice traps the ship; the crew demands to turn south, and Walton yields. Victor dies. The creature appears over his body, mourns, condemns himself, and vows to destroy himself on a funeral pyre before vanishing into darkness.

vocabulary.context: You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To free from encumbrance, or from anything which clogs, impedes, or obstructs
vocabulary.context: But this was not the time for delay: I disencumbered the dogs of their dead companion, gave them a plentiful portion of food; and, after an hour’s rest, which was absolutely necessary, and yet which was bitterly irksome to me, I continued my route.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil upon
vocabulary.context: Why do you not execrate the rustic who sought to destroy the saviour of his child?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of giving premature birth
vocabulary.context: I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To change from a fluid to a solid state by cold
vocabulary.context: You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To give feeble or scattered rays of light
vocabulary.context: Frankenstein has daily declined in health: a feverish fire still glimmers in his eyes; but he is exhausted, and, when suddenly roused to any exertion, he speedily sinks again into apparent lifelessness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: A mark in the skin or flesh of an animal, made by a wound or ulcer, and remaining after the wound or ulcer is healed
vocabulary.context: I approached this tremendous being; I dared not again raise my eyes to his face, there was something so scaring and unearthly in his ugliness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: You will find near this place, if you follow not too tardily, a dead hare; eat, and be refreshed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To form by putting together two or more things or parts
vocabulary.context: Oh, no! the only joy that he can now know will be when he composes his shattered spirit to peace and death.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To form, as sound, to a certain key, or to a certain portion
vocabulary.context: He spoke this with a voice so modulated to the different feelings expressed in his speech, with an eye so full of lofty design and heroism, that can you wonder that these men were moved?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: Walton's choice to return is a moral decision, contrasting with Victor's refusal to stop.

significance: The ending lets Walton learn the lesson, while the creature's final speech gives him the last eloquent word.
discussionQuestions: Does Walton learn from Victor? What evidence shows it?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Shelley show the final reckoning? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIV develops the idea of the final reckoning. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Chapter XXIV to complicate the reader's understanding of the final reckoning. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the final reckoning responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the final reckoning. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: What his feelings were whom I pursued I cannot know. Sometimes, indeed, he left marks in writing on the barks of the trees, or cut in stone, that guided me, and instigated my fury. “My reign is not yet over,” (these words were legible in one of these inscriptions;) “you live, and my power is complete. Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am impassive. You will find near this place, if you follow not too tardily, a dead hare; eat, and be refreshed. Come on, my enemy; we have yet to wrestle for our lives; but many hard and miserable hours must you endure until that period shall arrive.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXIV”?

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Does Walton learn from Victor? What evidence shows it? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include curdles, disencumbered, execrate, abortion, congeal. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To change into curd.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Walton's choice to return is a moral decision, contrasting with Victor's refusal to stop. Now, why does this chapter matter? The ending lets Walton learn the lesson, while the creature's final speech gives him the last eloquent word. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot point of view, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.

segments.script: To close: in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the final reckoning, and back it with one short quotation. Hand it to me on your way out.
